title: Adaptive Kernel Design for Bayesian Optimization Is a Piece of CAKE with LLMs
description: CAKE uses large language models as genetic operators to evolve Gaussian-process kernels for adaptive, data-efficient Bayesian optimization.

hero.alt: CAKE workflow: an initial population of Gaussian-process kernels undergoes LLM-guided crossover and mutation, fitness evaluation, and survivor selection to produce an improved population.
hero.caption: Starting from an initial kernel population, CAKE uses the LLM for crossover and mutation, evaluates the proposed kernels by fitness, and advances the fittest candidates to the next generation before selecting the next BO query with BAKER.

abstract: The efficiency of Bayesian optimization (BO) relies heavily on the choice of the Gaussian process (GP) kernel, which plays a central role in balancing exploration and exploitation under limited evaluation budgets. Traditional BO methods often rely on fixed or heuristic kernel selection strategies, which can result in slow convergence or suboptimal solutions when the chosen kernel is poorly suited to the underlying objective function. To address this limitation, we propose a freshly-baked Context-Aware Kernel Evolution (CAKE) to enhance BO with large language models (LLMs). Concretely, CAKE leverages LLMs as the crossover and mutation operators to adaptively generate and refine GP kernels based on the observed data throughout the optimization process. To maximize the power of CAKE, we further propose BIC-Acquisition Kernel Ranking (BAKER) to select the most effective kernel through balancing the model fit measured by the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) with the expected improvement at each iteration of BO. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our fresh CAKE-based BO method consistently outperforms established baselines across a range of real-world tasks, including hyperparameter optimization, controller tuning, and photonic chip design.

sections.title: Context-Aware Kernel Evolution
sections.lead: CAKE refines the Gaussian-process kernel before choosing every new Bayesian optimization query.

blocks.text: CAKE begins from a small set of randomly sampled observations and a population of six base kernels: squared exponential (SE), periodic (PER), linear (LIN), rational quadratic (RQ), Matérn-3/2 (M3), and Matérn-5/2 (M5). The observations are inserted into a system prompt as few-shot examples. The LLM is asked to act as a Gaussian-process expert, analyze patterns in the observed data, and reason about kernel structures that could explain them. This operates entirely in context and does not fine-tune or update the LLM.

Each candidate is a compositional kernel built with addition and multiplication, operations that preserve kernel validity. Its fitness is derived from the Bayesian information criterion (BIC), which balances Gaussian-process model fit against complexity, and is normalized to [0, 1] across tasks.

items: Condition on the current observations: at every BO iteration, CAKE updates the prompt with all input–output pairs collected so far.

Crossover: five times per iteration, two parent kernels are sampled with probability proportional to fitness. The LLM combines them using addition or multiplication and explains the proposed structure.

Mutation: with probability 0.7, the LLM modifies the fittest kernel by replacing one base component with another. The crossover and mutation candidates are evaluated together with the existing population.
Survivor selection: CAKE retains the ten kernels with the highest normalized BIC fitness to form the next generation.

Rank and query: BAKER weights each surviving kernel in proportion to exp(−BIC), multiplies that weight by the normalized expected improvement at the kernel’s proposed query, and selects the highest-scoring kernel–query pair. The objective is evaluated and the new observation is added before the loop repeats.

blocks.text: BAKER is important because the best-fitting kernel does not necessarily propose the most useful next evaluation. Its joint ranking explicitly balances model fit with the potential optimization gain of the candidate query.

sections.title: Experimental Evaluation
sections.lead: The evaluation spans heterogeneous hyperparameter landscapes, dynamic control environments, and multi-objective physical design.

blocks.text: All experiments use BoTorch, with expected improvement as the default acquisition function and gpt-4o-mini as the LLM. CAKE is compared with fixed kernels; adaptive kernel selection using Random, Utility, or BIC criteria; deep and ensemble Gaussian processes; Compositional Kernel Search (CKS); and Automated Bayesian Optimization (ABO). Shaded regions in the plots denote standard error over independent trials.

For hyperparameter optimization, HPOBench supplies 60 tasks from 12 OpenML datasets and five model families: logistic regression, support vector machines, random forests, XGBoost, and multilayer perceptrons. Each model–dataset pair is optimized for test accuracy over 100 trials and 20 random seeds. CAKE achieves the highest average test accuracy for all five model families. The advantage is especially visible early in optimization: averaged across HPOBench, CAKE realizes 67.5% of its eventual improvement within the first quarter of the budget and more than 83% by the halfway point.

blocks.alt: Five learning curves for logistic regression, SVM, random forest, XGBoost, and MLP; the black CAKE curve finishes above all comparison methods in every panel.
blocks.caption: Average test accuracy over 20 random seeds. CAKE is the black curve; shaded regions show standard error.

blocks.text: The controller experiments test adaptation under changing environments. Robot pushing optimizes 14 controller parameters governing two robotic hands, while lunar landing optimizes 12 parameters that map an eight-dimensional state to four actions. Both tasks run for 1,000 iterations and are averaged over ten initial conditions. CAKE obtains the highest average reward in both tasks and converges fastest on robot pushing. In lunar landing, ABO is the only baseline that also reaches the target reward of 200, but its performance fluctuates more than CAKE across difficult environments; fixed SE and M5 kernels tend to plateau earlier.

blocks.alt: Reward curves for robot pushing and lunar lander; the black CAKE curve ends highest in both panels and exceeds the lunar-lander target score of 200.
blocks.caption: Controller tuning over 1,000 iterations, averaged across ten initial conditions.

blocks.text: Photonic chip design is formulated as a multi-objective black-box problem with five competing physical indicators: Q-factor, wavelength, lasing area, power, and divergence angle. CAKE is evaluated for 250 trials over ten random initializations using expected hypervolume improvement, against Single-Task GP, Additive GP, CKS, and ABO. It achieves the highest overall score and hypervolume, indicating both a stronger design and broader exploration of the Pareto front. A substantially higher-scoring solution appears in fewer than 40 trials, which the paper reports as a tenfold acceleration of the design cycle relative to the baselines.

blocks.alt: Photonic-chip optimization curves for score and hypervolume; the black CAKE curve rises fastest and finishes highest in both panels.
blocks.caption: Average score and hypervolume across 250 trials for the multi-objective photonic-chip task.

sections.title: What Drives the Improvement?
sections.lead: Ablations separate the contribution of LLM-guided kernel evolution from BAKER’s joint model-fit and acquisition ranking.

blocks.text: Across all 60 HPOBench tasks, the complete CAKE + BAKER configuration obtains the best average rank, 1.04. Selecting CAKE kernels with acquisition utility alone ranks second at 2.40, while a conventional genetic algorithm reaches 2.70 and CAKE with BIC alone reaches 3.02. CKS + BAKER, Adaptive + BAKER, and random recombination rank 3.12, 4.60, and 6.80, respectively. Removing either the LLM-guided evolution or BAKER therefore degrades performance.

blocks.text: The population analysis provides a mechanism-level view of this gain. After one LLM edit—one crossover and mutation round—the fitness distribution already shifts toward stronger kernels. After five and ten edits, mean fitness continues to rise and variance narrows. Random recombination and traditional genetic operators converge more slowly and retain broader, lower-fitness distributions.
